Getting started with toad

Source: vignettes/toad.qmd

What toad does

{toad} (Tractography Open Atlas Data) provides easy access to reference white matter tractography atlases for benchmarking and anomaly-detection studies of brain microstructure. It is the data layer of the {tractoverse} package family: bundles are returned as the S7 streamline, bundle, and bundle_set classes of the {fiber} package, so they plug directly into fiber’s shape-descriptor tools, riot’s file readers/writers, and rtists’ visualisation.

Two atlases are available:

Dataset What it contains License
HCP1065 Population-averaged atlas, 87 white matter bundles from 1,065 HCP subjects CC BY-SA 4.0
TractSeg Per-subject segmentations, 72 tracts in 105 HCP subjects CC BY-NC 4.0 — non-commercial

The data are hosted as GitHub releases in the package repository and are downloaded on demand as fiber::bundle objects — no bulky data files are bundled with the package itself.

The central functions are:

  • available_datasets() — the datasets a given toad version can access;
  • available_bundles() — the bundles available within a dataset;
  • import_bundle() — download a bundle (or several) as a fiber object.

The two datasets

HCP1065 population-averaged atlas

The HCP1065 atlas is a whole-brain population-averaged tractography atlas derived from 1,065 healthy adults of the Human Connectome Project Young Adult dataset. It contains 87 white matter bundles, each stored as a single population-level bundle.

The atlas is distributed under the CC BY-SA 4.0 license. Please cite the original work when using it:

Yeh FC. Population-based tract-to-region connectome of the human brain and its hierarchical topology. Nat Commun 13, 4933 (2022). https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-022-32595-4

TractSeg per-subject bundles

The TractSeg dataset provides per-subject white matter bundle segmentations of 72 tracts in 105 HCP Young Adult subjects, generated with TractSeg and redistributed from the Zenodo archive (DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.1477956). Because the segmentations are per-subject, this dataset supports population-style analyses (e.g. bundle shape across subjects), not just single population averages.

The data are distributed under the CC BY-NC 4.0 license — non-commercial use only. Please cite the original TractSeg publication:

Wasserthal J, Neher P, Maier-Hein KH. TractSeg — Fast and accurate white matter tract segmentation. NeuroImage 183, 239–253 (2018). https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuroimage.2018.07.070

Both datasets originate from the Human Connectome Project; users must also comply with the HCP data-use terms.

Discovering datasets and bundles

available_datasets() returns the names of the datasets toad can access:

available_datasets()
#> [1] "HCP1065"  "TractSeg"

available_bundles() gives the full names of the bundles in a dataset — the values to pass to the bundle argument of import_bundle():

hcp_bundles <- available_bundles("HCP1065")
length(hcp_bundles)
#> [1] 87
head(hcp_bundles)
#> [1] "Anterior Commissure"            "Left Arcuate Fasciculus"       
#> [3] "Right Arcuate Fasciculus"       "Left Acoustic Radiation"       
#> [5] "Right Acoustic Radiation"       "Left Frontal Parietal Cingulum"
ts_bundles <- available_bundles("TractSeg")
length(ts_bundles)
#> [1] 72
head(ts_bundles)
#> [1] "Left Arcuate Fasciculus"           "Right Arcuate Fasciculus"         
#> [3] "Left Anterior Thalamic Radiation"  "Right Anterior Thalamic Radiation"
#> [5] "Commissure Anterior"               "Corpus Callosum"

Importing bundles

import_bundle(dataset, bundle, subjects = NULL) downloads the requested bundle from the GitHub release associated with the dataset and returns it as a fiber::bundle:

cst_left <- import_bundle("HCP1065", "Left Corticospinal Tract")
cst_left

Each bundle also ships a convenience accessor, so import_bundle("HCP1065", "Left Corticospinal Tract") is equivalent to HCP1065_CST_L()

identical(cst_left, HCP1065_CST_L())

Controlling subjects (TractSeg)

For multi-subject datasets, the subjects argument controls which subjects are loaded. It takes four forms:

subjects Result
NULL (default) All available subjects, as a bundle_set
an integer scalar n n random subjects, as a bundle_set
a character vector Those subject IDs, as a bundle_set
a character scalar That single subject, returned directly as a bundle 
# A single subject — returns a bundle
af_left <- import_bundle(
  "TractSeg",
  "Left Arcuate Fasciculus",
  subjects = "599469"
)
af_left
# A random sample of 10 subjects — returns a bundle_set
af_sample <- import_bundle("TractSeg", "Left Arcuate Fasciculus", subjects = 10L)
af_sample
# Specific subjects by ID — returns a bundle_set
af_two <- import_bundle(
  "TractSeg",
  "Left Arcuate Fasciculus",
  subjects = c("599469", "613538")
)
af_two

The convenience accessors accept the same argument, e.g. TractSeg_AF_left(subjects = 10L).

Bundle objects

Whatever the dataset, import_bundle() returns objects defined by the {fiber} package:

  • a streamline holds one fibre tract: @points is an n×3n \times 3 numeric matrix with columns X, Y, Z; @point_data is a named list of per-point scalar attributes; @streamline_data is a named list of per-streamline scalars;
  • a bundle is an ordered collection of streamlines in @streamlines, plus optional bundle-level metadata in @bundle_data;
  • a bundle_set is a named collection of bundles, with the input names preserved in @bundle_data$id_from_input_names.

For example, the metadata attached by toad to each imported bundle tells you where it came from:

cst_left@bundle_data

Everything else — shape descriptors, reparametrisation, Hausdorff distances — happens with the tools described in the fiber vignette.

Where to go next

  • The toad API vignette describes the package’s internal functions and the GitHub-releases data architecture in detail.
  • The {fiber} package provides the streamline, bundle, and bundle_set classes.
  • The other tractoverse packages ({riot} for input/output, {rtists} for visualization, {bot} for optimal transport of bundles) build on the same data model.
